segments.vo: Eight hundred forty-seven million dollars. One ticket. One person.

On Wednesday, November fourth, a single Powerball ticket sold in New Jersey matched every number. An eight hundred forty-seven million dollar jackpot. The tenth-largest in Powerball history. The odds were one in two hundred ninety-two million.
But here's the thing nobody tells you. The winner is not getting eight hundred forty-seven million dollars. Not even close.

So how much do they actually keep? Should they take the lump sum or the payments? And stay to the end, because I'll show you what happens if you put six dollars a week into the stock market instead of lottery tickets. Since the year 2000.

First problem. That eight hundred forty-seven million is the annuity. Thirty payments, spread over twenty-nine years. If you want the money now, the cash value is about three hundred sixty-three million dollars. Less than half.

And the annuity isn't thirty equal checks. Each yearly payment is five percent bigger than the last, so the early checks are the smallest. That's why most big winners take the cash, even though it's less than half.

Second problem. Taxes. The IRS withholds twenty-four percent up front. But a prize this big lands in the top federal bracket, thirty-seven percent. That's about one hundred thirty-four million dollars.

Then New Jersey. The state withholds eight percent on any lottery prize over five hundred thousand dollars, and its top income tax rate is ten point seven five percent. That's about thirty-nine million more.

scene.source: NJ Division of Taxation; NBC Philadelphia

segments.vo: So here's the real number. Start with eight hundred forty-seven million. Take the cash, pay the taxes, and you're left with roughly one hundred ninety million dollars. About twenty-two cents of every headline dollar. Rough math, before any deductions or planning.

Now, let's be fair. A hundred ninety million is still insane money. How insane? If you earned one hundred thousand dollars a year, it would take you about one thousand eight hundred ninety-seven years to earn that. You'd have to start working around the year one hundred thirty A D.

Okay. Time for the data. What are your chances of being that person? One in two hundred ninety-two million. Say you buy one ticket for every drawing. Three drawings a week, every week. On average, you'd expect to hit the jackpot once every one point eight seven million years.

Here's the part most headlines skip. The jackpot is designed to grow. Every drawing with no winner makes it bigger, the bigger number makes the news, and the news sells more tickets. That loop is how jackpots get this big. The biggest one ever, two point zero four billion dollars, was won by a single ticket in California in November 2022.

And now, the moment I promised. Say instead of lottery tickets, you put six dollars a week, that's about a dollar twenty every trading day, into a boring S and P five hundred fund. Starting January 2000.

Not millions. But here's the difference. Over long stretches like this one, the boring stock plan has usually ended up ahead. The ticket plan almost never does.
So if you ever do win, what then? We don't give advice. But here are the three paths winners usually face.

One. Lump sum. Pay the tax now, invest the rest, and it's on you. Two. Annuity. Thirty payments, a built-in guard against spending it all in a year. Three. Lawyers first. Many experts say: before you claim, get a lawyer, an accountant and a financial planner, and stay quiet if your state allows it.
